newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr suffers jobs blow, not mortal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr suffers jobs blow, not mortal.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a step back Thursday as a soft set of jobs data provided the excuse for a bout of profit-taking on recent lucrative gains.

The market had been inclined to sell when the week's 3/4 cent rally faltered at US$0.7960 chart resistance. The impulse gathered pace when employment data for February showed a surprise 7,200 fall, stirring doubts about whether another rate cut was really the impossibility many imagined.
Analysts felt the corection could run deeper yet but would not end the uptrend. "The A$ revival may suffer the odd ripple on weak data, but at core will be resilient," said Citibank.
"Despite the still-strong U.S. dollar, the Aussie will soon be testing 80 cents," said Annette Beacher, senior economist at Citibank Australia.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) it had recoiled to US$0.7911/16 from an early US$0.7951/56 and US$0.7941/46 late here Wednesday.
Some sort of a pullback had always been on the cards given the currency had climbed 3/4 cent this week alone and was up over five percent since troughing at US$0.7550 on February 12.
Support had so far proved solid at US$0.7910 with some good U.S. names on the bid, but analysts reckoned the correction could extend to US$0.7835 without endangering the uptrend.
The currency also ran into profit-taking on some major crosses, particularly the mark and Swiss franc which were enjoying a rare bounce on all exchanges.
It also dipped to 96.66/76 yen from Wednesday's 4-1/2 year closing high of 97.45/55, partly as speculation of a rush of new dual currency samurai demand was disappointed.

Traders said speculators had got a little worked up after Nomura launched a 30 billion yen/A$ bond Wednesday, the first since early January, and went long of AUD/yen in anticipation of more. Their ardour appeared premature as dealers reported not a whiff of an issue and positions were cut as the dat progressed.
All this took a 0.2 point bite out of the trade weighted index leaving it at 60.8, but that was hardly weak given Wednesday's 61.0 finish had been a six-year high.
Much of the dollar's recent strength reflected the receding risk of another easing after the Reserve Bank voiced an upbeat view on the economy and leading economic data turned firmer.

Today's soft employment numbers might just be seen seen as a threat to the steady rate case, analysts warned, particularly as Prime Minister John Howard said only yesterday the economy needed to grow faster to reduce unemployment. The February figures showed the jobless rate rising to 8.8 percent from 8.6.
Even the breakdown was poor with full-time jobs diving 24,200 while lower paid, less secure part-time employment continued last year's steady rise with a 17,000 gain.

However, analysts noted employment was a lagging indicator on the economy and a more forward-looking snapshot was provided by housing finance commitments, also released today, which showed a strong 5.0 percent rise in January.
This came on top of a 5.0 percent gain in December and took total commitments to their highest level since July 1994.
The value of commitments also rose a robust 10.5 percent to A$4.61 billion, the largest monthly amount since records began.

The gains boded well for increased retail spending on large household items while a 6.1 percent rise in finance for the construction of new dwellings suggested employment in the housing industry should be on the way up.
There was also upbeat news from a Westpac survey of business confidence which revealed a distinct lift in confidence and output expectations for the coming June quarter.
The net balance of respondents expecting an improvement in business conditions over the next six months rose to 26 percent in the March quarter from 13 percent the quarter before.
